about: Every claim this project makes about itself, with the state of the thing claimed, where its numbers came from, and the file that proves it. The two state vocabularies are the ones in src/model/capability.ts and nowhere else, so a state cannot appear here that the interface pages do not also know. Checked by tests/unit/claims.test.ts, which fails if a state is invented, an id repeats, or an evidence path does not exist on disk.
null_data_means: Some claims are about the shape of this repository rather than about a measurement it displays. Those carry data: null and a why_no_data line, because stretching a data state to cover them would make the vocabulary mean less. See DECISIONS.md D-059.

claims.claim: HydraDB v0.1.1 is built from source and serves this project over its HTTP query API on loopback.
claims.reproduce: bash scripts/hydra-node.sh start && bash scripts/hydra-node.sh status
claims.caveat: The node runs on this machine. The public URL in the deployment claim below replays recorded answers from this node; it does not host one.

claims.claim: Which Cypher this engine accepts was established by running 162 probes against a live node, not by reading a compatibility table.
claims.caveat: Each record holds the query, the parameters, the HTTP status and the engine's own rejection text, unedited. The unsupported list in the integration doc is derived from these files rather than assumed.

claims.claim: The generated corpus loads into the graph as vertices and edges, and a second run adds nothing.
claims.caveat: The corpus is generated by this repository. It is a synthetic workplace history with known answers, which is what makes the evaluation checkable, and it is not anybody's real messages.

claims.claim: The verdict on a question is decided by which edges exist between claims. No model reads the stored text.
claims.caveat: Deterministic means the same graph gives the same verdict, not that the verdict is right about the world. What it is right about is the corpus, which is what the evaluation measures.

claims.claim: Over 60 questions covering eight kinds of thread, every answer matched the expected one.
claims.caveat: 60 questions over one generated corpus. A hundred per cent on a set this size is a statement about this corpus and this question set, not a general accuracy figure.

claims.claim: When the graph does not support an answer, the system says which of the five absences it is instead of answering.
claims.caveat: Same 60 question set as the evaluation claim. The five absences are named in the interface, and each one points at the read that came back empty.

claims.claim: Against five flat retrieval approaches over 51 configurations, the best configuration of hybrid retrieval with two hop expansion and conflict handling scores the same as this system. On correctness it is a tie.
claims.caveat: This is a tie and is written as one everywhere it appears. The report says so in its own words: no claim of better recall or better abstention survives this run, and none is made. The difference that does survive is context size, 15 tokens against 636, and a graph read that returns the claim rather than the passages around it.

claims.claim: The unit suite covers the renderer, the resolver, the decoders, the voice machine, the CLI, the MCP adapter and this file, and it needs no database.
claims.caveat: Negative paths are asserted, so the run prints handled errors to stderr on purpose. A green summary line with error text above it is the expected shape.

claims.claim: The contract suite runs against the live node and fails if the wire shape or the Cypher subset moves.
claims.reproduce: bash scripts/hydra-node.sh start && npm run test:contract
claims.caveat: These skip rather than pass when no node is reachable. A run that reports skips is not a run that passed.

claims.claim: A fresh clone installs, typechecks, tests, ingests and answers, recorded end to end.
claims.caveat: The clone reads a local .env.local for its HydraDB token, so the transcript ends with an instruction to delete the clone.

claims.claim: The screenshot set is produced by one command against the running server, at three viewports plus full page, and every file is read back off disk and checked before the run is allowed to pass.
claims.caveat: Every image is a capture of this build serving the seeded corpus. None is a mockup and none was retouched. One capture asks Chrome for a light preference and comes back byte identical to its dark twin, because the page has one ground. See DECISIONS.md D-052 and D-059.

claims.claim: The package declares one runtime dependency, the official MCP SDK. Nothing the web server imports touches it.
claims.why_no_data: This is a fact about package.json, not a measurement the product displays.
claims.reproduce: node -e "const p=require('./package.json');console.log(p.dependencies)"  # then: grep -rn modelcontextprotocol src/server src/view src/retrieval src/hydra
claims.caveat: It was zero until the MCP server needed a spec-compliant transport, and writing one by hand would have been a worse answer than installing the maintained SDK. The dependency is confined to src/mcp and scripts/mcp.ts: the pages the judge opens still import nothing from node_modules at runtime and still ship no script.

claims.claim: No page ships a script. The policy that says so is served as a header and repeated in a meta tag.
claims.why_no_data: This is a fact about what the server emits, not a measurement.
claims.reproduce: npm run serve  # then: curl -sI http://127.0.0.1:3014/ | grep -i content-security-policy
claims.caveat: This is why the voice surface is reachable by URL rather than driven by a client. It is a constraint the design was fitted to, not a feature.

claims.claim: The voice interface exists as a finite machine with fourteen states, every one of which renders from the address bar. No audio is captured, transcribed or synthesised.
claims.reproduce: npm run serve  # then open /voice and follow any state link
claims.caveat: Two of the four pipeline stages are the product and run. Two are audio and are not installed, so their timing column prints UNAVAILABLE rather than an estimate. The design this was built from carried two timings; neither was measured here, so neither is printed.

claims.claim: Speech to text is chosen and not built. The intended component is whisper.cpp with a quantized small.en model, run on the machine.
claims.caveat: Named so its absence is on the record. See DECISIONS.md D-056 for why the local path was chosen over a hosted one.

claims.claim: Speech synthesis is chosen and not built. The intended component is Kokoro-82M, run on the machine.
claims.caveat: See DECISIONS.md D-056.

claims.claim: The hosted services that would make voice work today are named, and none of them is called by any code here.
claims.caveat: Each is metered and quota limited, which is the reason the local path is the intended one. AssemblyAI has no credential configured at all and is listed in NEEDS_VAIBHAV.md item 7. There is no HTTP client in this repository except the HydraDB one.

claims.claim: No language model is called anywhere in this project, in the demo path or outside it.
claims.caveat: This is a deliberate exclusion from PLAN.md rather than something unfinished. The retrieval result is the answer, which is what makes the evidence trail complete.

claims.claim: The MCP server speaks the protocol over stdio and over Streamable HTTP, to clients written here and to one that was not. The parity script's SDK client drives both transports end to end, and the MCP Inspector CLI at 2.2.0, a separate codebase, consumed the documented mcpServers config block, spawned the server through it, listed the tools and called lacuna_ask and lacuna_health over stdio, then listed and called again over HTTP. The two tools/list responses are byte-identical across transports and the answered values match the parity sweep.
claims.reproduce: npm run parity   # both transports end to end; the inspector commands are in the 2026-08-14e README
claims.caveat: The third-party client is the MCP Inspector's CLI run from a terminal, not an editor or agent runtime. No interactive host has held a session with this server, so nothing on this line claims Claude Desktop or Cursor compatibility, and the server is not called universal. The inspector announces protocol 2025-11-25 against this server's 2025-06-18 and every call succeeded, which is version negotiation working, not a claim about either revision's full surface. The parity script's HTTP session was the SDK's Client over StreamableHTTPClientTransport, which validates structured output against each tool's outputSchema, so a successful call there is schema conformance rather than reachability.

claims.claim: The command line answers from the same live graph and prints the same typed result as JSON, both when a current claim exists and when the graph never stated one.
claims.caveat: Two subcommands of the several the binary carries were exercised this way. The JSON caps evidence at fifty items and reports the true count in evidenceTotal, so a caller reading the array length rather than that field would undercount. Nothing is published to a package registry and the exit codes are the only part of the surface a script should depend on so far.

claims.claim: MCP over stdio, MCP over its HTTP transport, and the command line return the same value for the same question, across all sixty gold questions from the evaluation plus two deep cases: same status, answer, reason code, claim id, superseded claims, evidence, evidence total, source state, and same set of graph reads with the same parameters and row counts.
claims.caveat: The check proves the three surfaces agree, not that the answers are right; judging answers against the gold expectations is npm run eval's job and is deliberately not duplicated here. The order the reads appear in the trace is excluded, because the reads are issued together and land as the node answers them, and reads with identical query text are tiebroken by their parameters, a fix the sweep's own first run forced. The two MCP surfaces share one tool implementation, so the HTTP case exercises the transport rather than the substance of the answer. The web pages share the resolver but are not part of this check.

claims.claim: A copy of the product is public at https://lacuna-five.vercel.app. It serves every page and answers every gold question from a recorded snapshot: replies a live HydraDB node produced at export time, stored byte for byte, decoded in production by the same client code the live server uses.

measured.csp: default-src 'none'; script-src 'none'; style-src 'self'; img-src 'self'; form-action 'self'; base-uri 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'

claims.reproduce: npm run serve:snapshot  # http://127.0.0.1:3015, same code and snapshot as the URL; npm run snapshot:verify replays all sixty gold questions
claims.caveat: The deployment is a replay, not a live node, and says so on its own pages. No writes happen there and no token is present there. The graph store limit below is why a long lived hosted node is still not honest; the snapshot is the honest shape a public copy can take today.

claims.claim: Writes to the local store stop working after enough of them, and the only remedy found is to move the store aside and reload.

measured.node_log: object store error: Operation put_opts with mode PutMode::Update not yet implemented by LocalFileSystem

claims.reproduce: bash scripts/hydra-node.sh stop && mv /var/lib/lacuna/hydradb/store /var/lib/lacuna/hydradb/store.wedged-$(date +%Y%m%d) && bash scripts/hydra-node.sh start && npm run ingest
claims.caveat: The unimplemented operation is now observed on the HTTP write path and not only in the collector loop, which is more than D-054 could say. It is still not established that the collector is what eventually kills writes, and the honest word for that is suspicion. A reset is not a fix: the replacement store runs on the same backend and should be expected to wedge again. Developing, testing and demoing are unaffected because the reset is cheap and the corpus reloads clean.

claims.claim: No credential is committed, in the working tree or anywhere in the history.
claims.why_no_data: This is a property of the repository, not a value any page shows.
claims.caveat: Two vendor keys are staged in a gitignored .env.local on the author's machine and no code here reads either. They should be revoked once the submission window closes. NEEDS_VAIBHAV.md item 8.

claims.claim: Text stored in the graph is rendered as data and never followed as instruction, because nothing in the answer path consults a model.
claims.caveat: The claim rests on the same fact as the llm-router entry: there is no model to inject into. Output escaping is a separate defence and is covered by the renderer tests.
